title: Minerals and Electrolytes

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of minerals like little building blocks that come from the earth, not something your body can build in its own kitchen. Vitamins are made of stuff living things put together, but minerals are simple earth-elements like iron and calcium. Since your body has no factory to make them, you have to eat them.

### Question 2

Some minerals your body needs by the spoonful, and some it needs by just a tiny pinch. The tiny-pinch ones are called trace minerals, like iron and zinc. 'Trace' means only a little, but even a little is really important, like a pinch of salt that changes a whole recipe.

### Question 3

Imagine each cell is a tiny water balloon. Sodium mostly floats in the water around the balloons, while potassium mostly stays inside them. Because sodium is the boss of the water outside, it decides how much water hangs around your cells.

### Question 4

Electrolytes are like tiny batteries dissolved in your body's water. They carry little sparks of electricity that tell your nerves to send messages and your muscles to squeeze. They also help decide where water goes, keeping everything balanced.

### Question 5

Plant iron comes in a 'locked' shape your gut has trouble grabbing. Vitamin C acts like a key that changes the iron into an 'unlocked' shape that slips right in. That is why a squeeze of lemon on your spinach helps you soak up more iron.

### Question 6

Bones are like concrete, and calcium and phosphorus are the two ingredients mixed together to make that concrete hard. They are both 'big helping' minerals your body needs a lot of, and they team up to build your skeleton and teeth.

### Question 7

The thyroid needs iodine to make its hormones, like a bakery needs flour to make bread. If iodine runs low, the thyroid works overtime and swells up trying to grab every bit it can, creating a lump in the neck called a goiter. That is why table salt has iodine added.

### Question 8

Iron helps your blood carry oxygen, like delivery trucks carrying air to every part of your body. Without enough iron, there are too few trucks, so you feel tired, look pale, and get out of breath easily. Plant foods have iron that is harder to absorb, so vegetarians have to be extra careful.

### Question 9

Too much sodium is like adding extra water to a garden hose, making the pressure inside push harder. Potassium works the opposite way, helping flush out extra sodium and letting the 'hose' relax. So eating less salty food and more fruits and veggies eases the pressure.

### Question 10

Sweat carries out both water and salt. If you only pour plain water back in, the salt left in your blood gets watered down too much, like weak soup. When blood salt drops too low, muscles cramp and the brain gets foggy, so athletes need drinks with electrolytes, not just water.

### Question 11

Eating calcium is only step one; your body still needs a doorman to let it into the blood, and that doorman is vitamin D. Without vitamin D, most of the calcium you eat walks right past the door and leaves your body. So the two must work as a team for strong bones.

### Question 12

Iron and zinc use the same narrow doorway to get into your blood. If a big crowd of iron shows up at once, it blocks the door so zinc can barely squeeze through. That is why taking large iron pills at the same time as zinc means you absorb less zinc.
